animals.name: Isaac Newton
animals.kennelCardMemo:
Gravity might pull things down, but this brilliant companion is all about elevating your mood. Isaac Newton is a dynamic canine thinker who arrived during the 2026 Texas floods and recently spent two weeks expanding his horizons in a foster sleepover. True to his namesake, his sharp intellect takes center stage, making him a quick study who reads human behavior and responds with a sweet, eager-to-please attitude. He turns daily interactions into engaging puzzles, thriving on activities that challenge his mind just as much as his body.

His playful, puppy-like energy fuels an absolute love for games of fetch, spirited matches of tug-of-war, and tracked-down squeaker toys. While he has a high-functioning brain, his calculations usually lead him right back to a cozy connection, as he frequently bypasses traditional boundaries to try and claim a spot right in your lap. He participates in shelter dog playgroups and maintains a highly affectionate, people-oriented focus. If you are looking for a clever, fun-loving partner to keep life interesting and your lap warm, this charming genius is ready to make the discovery of a lifetime. Meet Isaac Newton and bring him home today.

How long was your Sleepover
He is very intelligent. Quickly learned “sit” and would do so for us to put his leash on. He is good on a leash so far- no issues. Doesn’t seem to be reactive to dogs (curious about large ones, no real interest in small dogs). Also this dog smiles. We will try to get a good photo- it’s the first dog I saw who smiles like that. Might be hard of hearing on the right side. He has bite marks on that side of his head and neck, maybe related.

memos.Disclaimer:
“Fear-Anxiety-Stress” (FAS) is a term used to describe a dog’s response to situations that make them feel threatened, uncomfortable, or unsure.
- Fear is a natural response to something perceived as a threat. It’s an instinct that helps dogs survive, but when it becomes overwhelming or chronic, it can be problematic.
- Anxiety is the anticipation of a future threat, often manifesting as restlessness or hypervigilance.
- Stress is the body’s response to these emotions, and over time it can take a toll on a dog's physical and emotional well-being.
FAS behavior(s) can stem from various factors, including past traumatic experiences, lack of socialization, changes in environment, or inherent temperament.

Specific Behavior: Audrey is a fearful under-socailized dog who may look for opportunities to hide or get away from situations or interactions that are uncomfortable or scary to her.

Strategies for Managing and Supporting Dogs with Fear-Anxiety-Stress Behaviors
- Create a Safe Environment: Dogs thrive in stable environments. When you first bring your dog home, give them a quiet space where they can retreat and feel safe. Minimize loud noises and sudden changes in the household to reduce stress triggers. Set up a cozy spot with their bed, water, and toys. Gradually introduce them to new areas and people, always letting them explore at their own pace.
- Establish Routine and Predictability: Dogs with anxiety do best when they can predict what’s going to happen next. Establish a daily routine for meals, walks, and rest. Structure helps alleviate uncertainty, making your dog feel more secure in their new home.
- Gradual Exposure and Desensitization: If certain stimuli or situations trigger your dog’s fear or stress (such as loud noises or strangers), work on desensitization. This involves exposing them to the trigger in a controlled way, starting with very low-intensity versions and slowly increasing exposure as they become more comfortable. Always pair these exposures with something positive to change their emotional response (like treats or play) and allow them to acclimate at their own pace.
- Provide Physical and Mental Stimulation: Physical activity helps reduce stress and expend excess energy, so ensure your dog has a consistent form of physical activity that feels safe and comfortable to them. Engaging your dog’s mind with interactive puzzle toys, training games, or scent work can also help reduce anxiety by giving them a constructive way to channel nervous energy. Boredom can worsen FAS, so keeping your dog mentally stimulated is important for managing stress.
- Consider Calming Aids or Supplements: There are various natural supplements and calming products designed to help dogs with stress. Some examples include pheromone diffusers like Adaptil, therapeutic techniques like T-Touch, massage, or acupuncture, and pressure wraps like Thundershirts. In severe cases, it’s worth consulting a vet or a behaviorist about additional treatments such as anxiety medications.
- Positive Reinforcement Training: Training through gentle and steady positive reinforcement builds trust and confidence in dogs with FAS. Reward any progress with calm, confident, and curious behavior with treats, praise, play, affection, or whatever your dog finds most rewarding, and celebrate the small victories. Avoid punishment, scolding, or rushing progress, as these can increase anxiety and make FAS worse.

animals.name: Limosaurus
animals.kennelCardMemo:
Life is full of wonderful surprises, and this cheerful boy is proof that the best things come in uniquely charming packages. Limosaurus is a young, fun-loving fellow who brings a burst of pure joy wherever he goes. He is a truly sociable companion who has a naturally cheerful approach to life, making him incredibly fun to be around. He navigates daily strolls with a wonderful, silly curiosity and already shows great habits on a leash, stopping predictably at crosswalks and avoiding barking at other people or dogs along the way.

When it comes to outdoor time, he enjoys a healthy mix of running around, investigating interesting scents, and chasing after tennis balls. He recently discovered the sheer happiness of the backyard zoomies, which is an absolute delight to witness. Yet, for all his youthful, high-energy enthusiasm outdoors, he has a wonderful ability to transition into relaxation. He is a genuine enthusiast of lounging in a sunny yard, and he even had a blast during his recent bath time.

What truly sets him apart is his affectionate, companionable soul. He is a devoted friend who loves nothing more than finding a way to lean close, resting his head right against his person to soak up human company. He is highly responsive to treats and is happily learning new skills and tricks at a steady pace. With his expressive ears, his endearing underbite, and his deeply sweet nature, he is ready to bring an abundance of unconditional love to a brand-new routine.

"Limosaurus is ready to bring a lifetime of smiles and goofy joy straight to your home!" Meet this wonderful boy today and see how beautifully he fits into your life.

memos.Sleepover notes:
Unfortunately, we may have to give Limosaurus back today. While he is an amazing, sweet, and fun loving dog who is very high energy, we don’t believe he is potty trained and has had about 4 accidents yesterday during the day and 2 this morning. Given that my party and I live in an apartment, it has become increasingly difficult to clean up especially with all of us having to work during the day. Unfortunately if left alone for even a few minutes he does have another accident.

We also don’t believe he is crate trained. While he enters the crate quickly, when we close the door he does seem to get a little anxious. Although we don’t keep him in there for long, just enough time for us to clean up the pee, he seems to have a hard time adjusting and does bark.

We genuinely love him so much and he deserves the world, but I don’t think we are the right people to care for him. Some positives, however, that we would love to highlight is how cuddly he is when he is sleeping. He will always find a way to put his head on you to rest. He’s so goofy on walks but he doesn’t bark at other people or dogs. He takes well to guidance on a leash and knows when to stop and go at a cross walk. He responds well to treats and is slowly learning tricks. He would do great with little kids and loves running outdoors!

animals.name: Nutmeg
animals.kennelCardMemo:
Spicing up the world with her quiet resilience, a handsome dog named Nutmeg is ready to bring a touch of warmth to a patient home. She stands out immediately with her gorgeous, richly textured coat of reddish-brown and dark brindle swirls, paired with highly expressive, semi-pricked ears that turn attentively toward every new sound. Arriving as a brave survivor during the 2026 Texas floods, this sweet girl is learning to navigate life with a beautiful blend of caution and curiosity.

While the bustling shelter environment can cause her to feel quite nervous, her true, bright personality shines through during quiet field trips to local parks. As she explores fresh air and grassy spaces, her natural intelligence and sweet curiosity take over, helping her overcome her initial hesitation. She is remarkably smart and exceptionally food-motivated, showing a keen interest in tasty treats that help build her confidence in new situations.

Caretakers note that she is incredibly brave, often choosing to step out of her comfort zone to gently approach people for affection. She benefits greatly from a slow, careful approach, rewards patience by opening up fairly quickly, and shows a deeply companionable nature once she feels safe. A calm, predictable household is exactly what this good-natured girl needs to truly blossom. Come down and meet Nutmeg to bring a lifetime of quiet devotion into your home today.

memos.Foster Notes:
[Return] Unscheduled return on 8/1/26 from foster.

"He did great the first week, no issues at all aside from picking up a few things that he shouldn't have. I cleared my living area of anything he could get his hands on and things were fine for a few more days. He then began shredding rugs and any appliance plugs he could get his hands on. He managed to pull my fridge away from the wall enough to chew out the wiring in the back of it. The rugs became a daily shred fest and I couldn't remove them (some were purchased just for him) because he slips around on hardwood and gets very frightened. I tried crating him but I only had a soft crate and he shredded it on the second day of use. This morning I was cleaning up the mess from the night before and while outside he pulled my deep freeze away from the wall and chewed out the wiring on it and pulled my screen door down. He was always very sweet and playful with me, but he got very aggressive with my only visitor my 67 year old mother. He seemed to do okay when I was gone during the day and that was up to a 7 hour stretch a few times. But if I came home and left in the evening even if just for an hour the destruction started.

He made no messes in the house and understood not to get on the furniture after pushing him back down just a few times the first two days. I think he just has some big separation anxiety that came out as he got more comfortable."

memos.Disclaimer:
The dog you are adopting or fostering has been rescued from one of our more under-resourced partner shelters and unfortunately has come to us with ticks on them. Rest assured that upon their arrival they were treated with Nexgard which will kill fleas within hours and the ticks within 24-48 hours. Often the dead tick will detach on its own, but not always and might require removal.

We understand that this can be concerning to bring into your home, but we have some ideas that have worked for other fosters and adopters previously. In order to limit the spreading of the ticks while they are dying we recommend keeping the dog in a spare bathroom, bedroom or a x-pen area for this initial period. This will help with clean-up if they are in a smaller space where it is easier to clean up afterwards. Additionally, baths can help with removing the ticks! Just be aware that after the first bath you’ll want to use water only so you aren’t stripping your dog’s coat of their naturally occurring oils which could make them itchy.

If you have any concerns about your resident dog getting ticks from your foster or adopted dog, please let us know and we can provide a single dose of tick meds for them as well while your new APA! dog is getting rid of their ticks.

memos.Disclaimer:
"Separation-related behavior" is a term used to describe when a dog becomes stressed, anxious, or panicked when left alone or when separated from their humans. This may lead to behaviors such as excessive barking, whining, destructive chewing, pacing, or even attempts to escape. The key thing to remember is that the dog isn’t trying to misbehave or “act out.” These behaviors stem from their anxiety and inability to cope with being alone.
There are several reasons dogs can develop separation-related behaviors, including:
- Past Experiences: Dogs who have been abandoned, rehomed multiple times, or left alone for long periods may develop separation-related behaviors due to past trauma.
- Changes in Routine or Environment: Major life changes, such as moving to a new home, a change in schedule, or the loss of a family member, can trigger separation-related behaviors in some dogs.
- Genetic or Temperamental Factors: Some dogs are naturally more prone to anxiety or attachment behaviors due to their breed, genetics, or early socialization.

Specific Behavior: Able to break out of crates with ease and even when they were reinforced. Foster attempted keeping him in her bathroom and he scratched at the door until his paws/nails were bleeding

Strategies for Managing and Supporting Dogs with Separation-Related Behaviors
- Create a Safe, Comfortable Space: Establish a designated space where your dog feels secure, such as a crate or a cozy corner of a room. Fill it with comforting items like a soft bed, toys, and even an article of your clothing with your scent. This can help your dog feel more secure when you leave.
- Gradual Desensitization: The goal is to slowly teach your dog that being alone is safe and okay. Start by practicing short, in-home separation by leaving your dog in a separate room for short periods to help them become comfortable with your absence. Once they reliably exhibit that they are comfortable doing this, move forward by practicing leaving the house for very short periods (a few minutes) and gradually increase the time. Make sure to return before they become anxious, reinforcing that you’ll always come back. Over time, they’ll learn to relax even when you’re not there.
- Positive Association with Alone Time: Make your departures a positive experience by giving your dog something they love, such as a puzzle toy filled with treats or a long-lasting chew. This will help them associate your leaving with something good.
- Don’t Make a Big Deal of Departures and Returns: Avoid dramatic goodbyes or enthusiastic reunions, as this can heighten your dog’s anxiety. Instead, keep arrivals and departures calm and low-key so your dog doesn’t get worked up when you leave or return.
- Exercise and Mental Stimulation: A tired dog is a calm dog. Ensuring that your dog gets plenty of physical exercise and mental stimulation before you leave can reduce their anxiety and make it easier for them to settle down. Walks, playtime, and interactive toys can all help tire them out.
- Use Calming Aids or Tools: There are various tools that can help reduce anxiety, including calming pheromone sprays, anxiety wraps (like ThunderShirts), or natural calming supplements. These can provide additional support during the training process.

memos.Disclaimer:
The dog you are adopting or fostering has been rescued from one of our more under-resourced partner shelters and unfortunately has come to us with ticks on them. Rest assured that upon their arrival they were treated with Nexgard which will kill fleas within hours and the ticks within 24-48 hours. Often the dead tick will detach on its own, but not always and might require removal.

We understand that this can be concerning to bring into your home, but we have some ideas that have worked for other fosters and adopters previously. In order to limit the spreading of the ticks while they are dying we recommend keeping the dog in a spare bathroom, bedroom or a x-pen area for this initial period. This will help with clean-up if they are in a smaller space where it is easier to clean up afterwards. Additionally, baths can help with removing the ticks! Just be aware that after the first bath you’ll want to use water only so you aren’t stripping your dog’s coat of their naturally occurring oils which could make them itchy.

If you have any concerns about your resident dog getting ticks from your foster or adopted dog, please let us know and we can provide a single dose of tick meds for them as well while your new APA! dog is getting rid of their ticks.

animals.kennelCardMemo:
If you're looking for a gentle, loving companion, Bagel might just be your perfect match.

Bagel is truly one of the sweetest dogs you'll ever meet. He's been through a lot, so he's understandably a little shy when meeting new people. But the moment you offer him a belly rub or a warm hug, you'll have a best friend for life. Once he trusts you, he'll happily stay by your side, soaking up all the love and affection he can get.

This handsome boy is the definition of a couch potato. He's calm, quiet, and easygoing, preferring cozy naps and cuddle sessions over long adventures. He doesn't need much exercise, making him an excellent companion for someone looking for a relaxed, low-maintenance buddy.

Bagel is also incredibly well-mannered. He rarely barks (I've only heard him bark once!), never whines, and has a peaceful presence that's hard not to fall in love with. While other dogs can make him a little nervous, he simply prefers to keep his distance. People, on the other hand, are his favorite. All he really wants is a safe home, a comfy couch, and someone to shower him with love.

If you're ready to open your heart to a sweet soul who will reward your kindness with endless loyalty and affection, Bagel is waiting to meet you.

animals.kennelCardMemo:
Beautiful Lady is a gentle Shepherd mix with a quiet heart and a lot of love to give—once you've earned her trust. She can be shy with new people at first and needs some time to warm up. Once she's comfortable, her tail starts wagging, she seeks out attention, and she'll happily lean into firm head and ear scratches from the people she trusts.

Her favorite place is outside! She loves running and playing chase and would thrive with a securely fenced yard. She's curious and athletic, so she'll need a family that's mindful of open doors and fences while she settles in.

Beautiful Lady is wonderfully quiet. She rarely barks, prefers sleeping on a rug or the floor, and rides nicely in the car. On walks, she's comfortable on a leash but is still learning good leash manners and loves stopping to investigate interesting smells.

Beautiful Lady isn't looking for someone who expects instant affection. She's looking for someone who understands that trust takes time, celebrates the little victories, and knows that the deepest bonds are often the ones that grow slowly. If you're patient, gentle, and willing to let her come to you at her own pace, you'll discover an incredibly loyal companion who quietly fills your life with love.

memos.Disclaimer:
"Flight Risk" is a term used to describe when dogs who may have a strong tendency to escape or run away when they feel scared, anxious, bored, or overstimulated. This behavior can be triggered by loud noises, unfamiliar environments, lack of engagement, something desirable, or even a sudden movement. While dogs are transitioning into a new environment or home, there is a higher likelihood to see escape attempts.

Specific Behavior: During transition phase my attempt to door dart or look for weak points in a backyard fence. Should be closely monitored near doorways and in the backyard. Drag leash for first week in a new home.

Strategies for Managing and Supporting Dogs who Present a Flight Risk
- Secure Environment: Ensure that your home and yard are escape-proof. This means checking fences for any gaps or weaknesses, making sure gates latch securely, and being mindful of any potential escape routes. Consider adding additional barriers, like baby gates or temporary fencing, to further secure the area.
- Leash and Tethering: Keep a drag leash clipped to your dog’s collar for at least the first month while your dog is acclimating to their new home. When outside, always keep your dog on a leash, even in a fenced yard, until you are confident in their ability to stay within the boundaries. Do not leave them unattended when outside. A double-leash system (using both a harness and a collar) can provide extra security during walks, and a martingale collar will prevent him from being able to slip out and away. Avoid using a retractable leash, as they can easily break.
- Safe Entry and Exit: Be cautious when opening doors, as many flight-risk dogs may seize any opportunity to dart outside. Teach your dog to wait calmly before doors are opened, and set up gates or other air lock systems around exterior doors and gates to prevent door darting. When going on car rides, tether his leash outside of the door to ensure you can get a firm hold on it before opening the door. Do not leave windows open in the car during car rides, and never allow him to be off-leash in public.
- Identification & Tracking: Ensure your dog is always wearing a collar with up-to-date identification tags. Microchipping is also highly recommended as an additional layer of security, as well as attaching an Apple Airtag to their collar.
- Training and Positive Reinforcement: Work on building a strong recall response within him where he will reliably return to you when prompted.

7/22 - "Tentative / skittish to new people. Takes at least 10 mins, with men, maybe an hour in a safe area.

Meeting others, adolescent and women do better, grown men she’s slow to allow

Once bonded/comfortable, she seeks and leans in on pets, more head and ear oriented, doesn’t roll over for belly rubs, but will lift leg a little on side

She takes a while to warm up. But once she does she’s wagging her tail and coming up for attention.

She’s happiest outside, loves to play chase, as the chaser or the chase-ee

She loves strong head pets from those she trusts… it takes a while for her to ease into it.

She does not bark. Barely makes any sounds. Light whine, a slight growls sound once.

She wants OUT of the house. At the front door she eyes the door like a running back looking for a hole. In the back, she assesses my low chain link fence as a challenge. I blocked the view at the interesting spots and she’s less concerned. As we bond, she looks less.

She signals poorly for going outside for bathroom needs. She will lightly nose me, and get anxious and walk around… but that’s a lot like, hey, I’m bored, let’s play style. Now if I get anything I just let her outside. Too many accidents otherwise

I tested her on the dog door, but she’s not used to one.

She’s used to a leash, but is not “proper” leash trained. She wants to lead, but will stay within the lead length so if you hold it short, she’ll stay with it. She needs medium pressure to pull her back if she goes too far.

She responds to normal come and here type words, she gets intent

She is hard to pull from something when her nose grabs on to a smell, wait it out.

Only prey drive I’ve caught is a squirrel… she lunged, but stopped at the end of the leash… didn’t pull me hard.

Haven’t seen a cat on walks.

Her interest in other dogs is mostly, noting and tracking that they are there.

She seems to like to sleep on the floor, prefers a rug, not adverse to wooden floor. Will not join on couch or bed.

Doesn’t fetch, knows the tennis ball and ran over to look at it but left it.

Had a minute of interest in a tug rope… but didn’t and doesn’t care anymore

Ate a bully stick with excitement

Kind of knows some miscellaneous lay down/sit etc commands, but not clear.

Dog is ok in car… back seat in SUV unconstrained, was up some but when bored laid down

Housetraining… I think she’s mostly used to being outside. She signals very lightly to go outside. Like a nose bump and some room walking circles. She’s pooped inside and is horrified/guilty about it. This is an area to sort out."

She will come up to sniff but is skittish and will move away if there are sudden movements or boisterous conversation. She's jumpy on walks when cars/trucks rattle or squeak as they drive by.
Has been fine at home for a 5 hour absence. JA

animals.name: Cartoonishly Masculine
animals.kennelCardMemo:
Loving, Curious, Content

Cartoonishly Masculine may have a larger-than-life name, but his personality is pure sweetheart. This big-hearted orange tabby has adorable tiger stripes, soulful green eyes, and a striped tail worthy of its own dramatic entrance. His slightly shorter front legs even give him a touch of Puss in Boots charm.

Most of all, Cartoonishly Masculine has enough affection to brighten every day. His favorite place is wherever you are, and he will happily cuddle, make biscuits, or purr beside you while you work, read, or relax. He does not demand constant attention; he is simply content to share your space and gaze at you with those wonderfully expressive green eyes. When he does speak, his tiny mew is an adorable surprise.

He has just the right amount of playful energy, too. Ribbon toys, little fish, toy mice, and watching the world through the window are all high on his list of favorite activities. Curious and easygoing, he is genuinely happy simply spending time with his people.

Cartoonishly Masculine is currently carrying a few extra pounds and would benefit from measured meals and regular playtime—something he will surely be enthusiastic about if it involves his favorite toys!

After a stressful rescue from a shelter affected by recent flooding, Cartoonishly Masculine settled into his foster home with remarkable ease, behaving as though he had lived there for years. He has responded warmly to every person he has met. His experience with children is unknown, but he's been interacting with his foster's dog and they do well together.

During his brief stay at the APA! cattery, he preferred having his own space around other cats, so any feline introductions should be slow and thoughtful.

If you’ve been hoping for a cat who simply loves being with you, Cartoonishly Masculine may be your perfect match. Whether you’re working from home or relaxing with a good book, he’ll be happiest purring nearby. Playful when the toys come out and peaceful when it’s time to settle in, this affectionate orange gentleman is genuinely delighted just to be part of your life.

All APA! cats are fully vetted, spayed or neutered, and have updated vaccines and a microchip. Lifetime support is offered by our Cat Behavior Team.

For further information or to meet Cartoonishly Masculine, please email adopt@austinpetsalive.org.

animals.name: Penelope
animals.kennelCardMemo:
This expressive girl has a way of looking right into your soul with her big brown eyes and magnificent, upright ears. Penelope is a sweet-natured companion who has shown a beautifully gentle and cooperative side during everyday care like nail trimmings. When she is feeling relaxed and ready to bond, she is happy to roll over and show you her belly for some gentle rubs, or offer up a few affectionate kisses. She has a welcoming attitude when visitors come by the house, making her a pleasant host for casual company.

On outdoor adventures, Penelope is already leash trained, though she is still learning how to navigate the busy world around her. She can be quite observant on trails, sometimes freezing to quietly watch passing runners or other dogs, while other times she is content to simply stroll past them without notice. Because of her curious nature and this thoughtful approach to new things, a home with a yard would suit her well. This gives her a secure space to explore at her own pace and lets her naturally bright curiosity shine as she gets comfortable.

This smart girl is already well on her way to being an excellent housemate since she is both house trained and crate trained. She settles smoothly into her crate at bedtime and whenever her people are out of the house. Being on the younger side, Penelope is full of happy potential and is actively working on channeling her youthful enthusiasm, focusing on manners like sitting, lying down, and keeping her paws on the floor instead of climbing onto furniture or people. She is a truly good-natured, joyful companion who brings a lot of heart to your daily routine.

"Penelope is ready to wag her adorable nubbin tail right out the door with you!" Meet this charming girl today and welcome a lifetime of sweetness into your home.

memos.Foster Notes:
Penelope is a 30lb, medium-sized, calm, submissive girl, who is always willing to show you her belly. She loves giving and receiving kisses and is easy to handle (carry her, clip her nails, touch her teeth).

Penelope isn't much of a barker but she will bark if there's a dog on TV or hears other dogs in the neighborhood. She's leash, house, and crate trained (crated during bedtime and when others not home).

Not sure how she gets along with kids or other dogs, as she lives with 2 adults and no other pets, but she does well with guests. From walks at the neighborhood trail, she's pretty nervous around runners and sometimes dogs (will freeze up and and watch them as they pass)...but also, other times, wouldn't notice other dogs. Overall, she's pretty skittish and would probably do best in a home with a yard, as she doesn't really pee/poop during walks...that is, if she doesn't refuse her walks haha.

Penelope is still pretty young and is still learning how to control her energy, as far as, not climbing on people/furniture and how to sit and lie down. As Penelope has gotten more comfortable around the house, she's starting to become a very curious girl and will occasionally grab items (not toys) for play.... otherwise, I wouldn't call her destructive at all but also wouldn't trust her in a room alone for too long.

Penelope doesn't shed too much and, from a quick hair pull, not a lot of hair comes off but you'll still see her hair on your clothes.

Otherwise, she's a very happy, very sweet girl, and has the cutest nubbin' tail! from Amy B. 8/3/26

physicalExams.subjective: Reason for being hospitalized: Inappetance, lethargy, fever, presumed protein losing nephropathy (likely secondary to tick borne disease).
physicalExams.objective: Condition at discharge: Eating approximately 30-40%, urinating normally, no vomiting or diarrhea
physicalExams.plan:
Brief summary of condition: Lethargy, fever, anorexia. Lab work most consistent with a protein losing nephropathy, likely secondary to  tick borne disease. 

Medications to be discharged with:
Rx Doxycycline  (100 mg/ml)- Give 2 ml PO SID (once daily) through 9/1 (antibiotic for tick borne disease)
Rx Enalapril (5 mg tablets)- Give 2 tablets PO SID (once daily) in EVENING through 9/1 (do not let discontinue unless directed by DVM). Medication to help with protein loss in urine.
Rx Entyce (30 mg/ml)- Give 2 ml PO SID for appetite stimulation x 3 days in PM. Give through 8/11. Appetite stimulant.

Other care instructions (nursing care, wound care, activity restriction, etc) :
- Okay to let her determine her own activity level.
- Ideally long term we would want her on a special diet to minimize protein loss through urine; however, right now we just want her eating more consistently.

Monitor for the following, alert clinic if:
- If not eating at all, worsening lethargy, warm to the touch, vomiting, diarrhea, etc. 

Approved onsite location: TLAC 

If foster is best, what is the urgency? (low, medium, high) high

Behavior concerns: very restraint sensitive for handling, friendly for pets (unable to do blood work or check temps w/out sedation)

Any zoonotic concerns (RW, DW, etc)? no

Recheck date:
Approx 8/19 (10 days)- In person recheck of weight, get update on appetite, overall condition, likely will need sedation to recheck temp, BG, blood pressure, if any additional diagnostics needed. Update med and diet plan pending exam findings.

Make available for adoption: yes *With medical consult

Ok to go to foster: yes

Ok for playgroup or group room (if not, then when)? no wait until clinically improving

Ok for playgroup assessment(if not, then when)? see above

Prognosis/Any change in life expectancy? 
Unknown at this time. Based on her history, exam and labwork findings, we are highly suspicious Iced Coffee has a protein losing nephropathy, which is condition where there is excessive protein loss through the kidneys, likely secondary to tick borne disease. We are treating her with an antibiotic to treat common tick borne diseases and a medication to hopefully minimize protein loss through her urine. If this disease is caused by a tick borne disease called Ehrlichia, then the prognosis for recovery is better, if it is secondary to Lyme disease, then her long term prognosis is much more guarded. For now we are focusing on trying to get her eating more consistently, she has been eating approximately 30% in the clinic. We are hoping that once she is comfortable again in your home she will start eating more consistently. Because of restraint sensitivity handling, it is very challenging to monitor certain parameters of hers (such as temperature or blood work) while in the clinic (without sedation). For now we are hoping to get her feeling better in your home and plan on rechecking her at the recheck exam in approximately 10 days. If she goes home and is doing worse (stops eating altogether, very lethargic, hot to the touch etc) please reach out to us sooner.

Is there anything a future adopter should know to set them up for success?
She has pretty intense separation anxiety. At first, she’d even bark even when I closed the door to use the restroom. Over the course of just a week, she became more desensitized and no longer barked when I was out of her line of sight. I’d leave for work everyday and watch her through a doggy camera - she would bark and whine for 5-10 minutes immediately after I left, but napped on the couch all day until I came back home. I would leave the TV on for her but she’d seriously just sleep the entire time I was gone!

If you live in an apartment, the barking might be something you should keep in mind. I did not have a crate so she roamed freely. Never had any issues with using the restroom inside, messing up my furniture, or anything.

She LOVES (!!!!!!) sniffing walks. She’s the type of dog that stops and sniffs every bush. Would tug when she saw another dog because she got excited, but stopped if I said “noooooo.” Super curious about everything!

I did notice that she’s scared of a lot of things (like doors) but became more confident in such a short period of time. Has the typical chihuahua shakes. Would periodically wheeze/cough a lot. animals.kennelCardMemo:
t is safe to say our naming department really missed the mark on this one. While his name might conjure up images of loud, high-flying stadium antics, this particular dog is not really like his name at all. Looking at him, you are immediately drawn to his striking appearance, defined by a stunning coat of dark brindle swirls and a beautiful face featuring one bright, soulful blue eye paired with a warm brown one. Arriving as a brave survivor during the 2026 Texas floods, this resilient fellow has shown a gentle, watchful nature from the moment he arrived. Instead of an explosion of high energy, he brings a quiet, grounded presence to the room.

The bustling environment of a busy shelter can feel overwhelming for him right now, but his quiet courage shines through his calm demeanor. He possesses a genuinely sweet disposition and a companionable spirit that emerges beautifully in quieter moments. Caretakers note that he is a gentle boy who is steadily coming out of his shell as he learns to trust his surroundings. He is simply looking for a peaceful, predictable environment where he can rest his head and truly unwind at his own pace.

A patient, low-stress household provides the perfect setting for this good-natured dog to blossom into a wonderful, steady companion. Every small step forward is a rewarding milestone for a sweet soul ready to leave his stormy past behind. Come down and meet T-shirt Cannon to bring a lifetime of quiet devotion into your home today.

animals.kennelCardMemo:
Meet Rebecca, a gentle, confident, and delightfully clever social butterfly who is an absolute gem of a dog! Smart, cheerful, and incredibly loving, she adores everyone she meets, including kids, visitors, and other doggy friends. One of her most charming quirks is her signature happy dance: she makes adorable yodeling sounds while helicoptering her tail!

Rebecca understands love and praise in both English and Spanish, and her cleverness shines through in everything she does.

In the home, Rebecca has a wonderful moderate energy level. She sleeps soundly in her crate, relaxes easily on car rides, and stays calm and relaxed when left alone.

Rebecca is currently recovering from a front paw wound, which is healing nicely. She is also practicing her leash skills with a drag leash and gaining more confidence every day.

Sweet, goofy, and endlessly smart, Rebecca is ready to bring joy, yodels, and unconditional love to a very lucky forever home!

Ask to meet Rebecca today!

animals.kennelCardMemo:
Truly "Juan in a Million"

If you have ever said, "I want to help the dog that needs me the most," Juan is waiting for you.

When Juan first came into our care after surviving the devastating 2026 flood disaster, he was heartbreakingly thin and suffering from severe skin issues. Yet, from the very moment he was rescued, this brave boy chose hope over fear. He is a true fighter, recovering quickly and showing us every single day what unconditional love looks like.

Juan has unique, stunning heterochromia, including a cataract in one eye that he cannot see out of. But don't let that fool you—he does not let his visual impairment or his past hardships slow him down for a second. He has the absolute best spirit, a heart of pure gold, and a surprising, radiant joy that shines through everything he does.

Why You'll Fall in Love with Him:

Joyful Walker: He absolutely loves going on walks to explore the world around him.

Happiest Tail: His tail wags non-stop, spreading happiness wherever he steps.

Sweet & Friendly: He greets every day, and every friend, with a gentle and loving nature.

A Resilient Soul: His friends affectionately call him "Juan in a Million" because of his unmatched sweetness and bravery.

Be Part of His Comeback Story
Juan has overcome the rising waters and the pain of neglect, but he needs one final miracle: a foster or adoptive home to show him he is safe forever. We are looking for an incredible human foster ready to open their heart to a dog who will give you endless devotion in return.

Juan is ready to leave his past behind. Are you his One in a Million?

Select at least three traits that best describe this dog:

What made you smile or laugh about them?
Goofyness. His love of toys.

Is there anything a future adopter should know to set them up for success?
He was scared of stairs, at least the outdoor cement ones. But with some coaxing he made it up. By the end of day 2 he had mastered the stairs!

Did good with a bath, will try to jump out but if you let him keep his head in your lap he'll mostly listen. He likes to try and sneakily step out but it helps if you you pull the shower curtain on the tub and he can't see out.

Physical touch is his love language. He wants to lay with you/ on you on the couch, he likes to be up against you! If he whines while you drive reaching a hand back calms him down (again, physical touch!). If he determines you've been on your phone too long, he'll scoot closer and try to capture attention with head nudges.

He actively watches TV, he paid particular attention to cowboys versus aliens.

Has very minor separation anxiety, and it doesn't last long. If you close a room door or walk out the front, he'll whine for a few minutes but then he goes and sits somewhere to wait for you.
*He was loose and alone on Saturday for 2 hours and laid at the door waiting. He was loose and alone today while I'm working and is still just laying at the door (approx 7 hours). Zero destructive behavior.

He's respectful of furniture, he'll let you know he wants to come up but if you tell him no and set his paws back down on the ground and respects that he's not allowed to come up. He was told no once for the bed and didn't try again. I invited/allowed him on the couch and he happily joined to snuggle!

He really likes giving kisses, but prefers if you take it slower on giving him some back!

He loves toys! Especially ones that squeak, he likes for you to throw it and then he'll bring it back to play tug of war with a playful growl and tail wagging. He does not know the drop command.

He's a good leash-walker, he doesn't pull. He walks in front of and beside you but doesn't pull on the leash at all.

Friendly with other dogs, likes to play. He does do some nose-nudges to other dogs which can sometimes annoy them.

He hasn't fully figured out mirrors or reflections in windows, and is very curious about the 'other dog' looking at him! He's a silly guy.

Negative: He's a big licker, and also tries to hump (both myself and another male dog he met).

Tolerant

animals.name: Sammie
animals.kennelCardMemo:
Sammie is a 6-year-old gentleman who is the ultimate low-maintenance, gentle companion. Equal parts chill couch potato and fun-loving goofball, Sammie is a master at matching your energy. If you want to play, he’s ready to play, and if you want to lounge, he’s happiest snoozing right beside you on the couch or dog bed.

One of his most charming quirks is his adorable toy routine: he’ll wake up from a nap, march over to a toy, give it a few enthusiastic "shakes," and then go right back to relaxing. He’s a total social butterfly who loves everyone he meets, gets along wonderfully with other dogs, and walks nicely on a loose leash (though he prefers shorter, leisurely strolls as he builds up his Texas stamina!).

In the home, Sammie is an easygoing sweetheart who handles bath time like a champ and settles down comfortably when left alone.

If you’re looking for a sweet, adaptable, and loving boy who will shower you with affection and fit effortlessly into your routine, Sammie is ready to give his heart to you!

Inquire today to meet this sweet boy.

Confident, Inquisitive, Charming

Meet the beautiful and daring Night Court!

Night Court approaches life with confidence and curiosity. New places don't faze her! Instead, she's eager to explore every nook and cranny before finding the perfect spot to relax. Once she's satisfied her adventurous side, she's content to lounge nearby, keeping a watchful eye on whatever you're doing.

She's an expressive girl who loves carrying on conversations with her people, using a variety of adorable chirps and meows to share her thoughts throughout the day. She also enjoys following her favorite humans from room to room and never says no to a fishy treat or a play session with a wriggling wand toy. Night Court would thrive in a home where she has plenty of space to roam and people to keep her company, as being isolated makes this social butterfly anxious.

All APA! cats are fully vetted, spayed or neutered, and have updated vaccines and a microchip. Lifetime support is offered by our Cat Behavior Team.

animals.name: Magic
animals.kennelCardMemo:
It is impossible to look at Magic without being spellbound by those piercing, ice-blue eyes set against a sleek black tuxedo coat. This young girl turns heads wherever she goes, showing off her striking looks, white paws, and a sweet, dusting of white across her muzzle. While she brings plenty of happy puppy energy to playtime, her real superpower is how quickly she settles into a calm, content rhythm when hanging out by your side. She approaches the world with a happy, confident demeanor that instantly puts everyone at ease.

True to her name, Magic makes everyday outings look effortless. On an off-campus trip to a local brewery she proved to be a social star, greeting new people with a rapidly wagging tail and soaking up all the pets she could get while resting quietly under the table during dinner. She walks beautifully on a leash, staying right with her handler and completely ignoring outside distractions, even when other dogs get vocal. Whether she is exploring a new patio, playing with fellow dogs, or just enjoying a quiet moment, Magic brings a bit of effortless joy wherever she goes.

Select at least three traits that best describe this dog:

What made you smile or laugh about them?
She's a doll. She has an adorable slight underbite. She's figuring out what living in a house is like. I don't think she's been in one before. She loves soft toys. She has picked out a carrot, a donut and a strawberry. She walks around with her strawberry regularly. She didn't respond to Claudette at all, so I made up the name Claudelie and she likes it.

Is there anything a future adopter should know to set them up for success?
This was reported to Dog Support: There is something wrong with her front right shoulder, possibly her leg. She moves like she had an injury that healed, but didn't heal well. Her right shoulder and leg are underdeveloped in comparison to the left side of her body. She doesn't seem to be in any pain. I touched her shoulder and down her leg and she didn't wince or get scared, but she will not put all of her weight on her right leg.

She gets along with our adopted shepherd and our four cats. Sugar Cookie, our shepherd, was adopted from Tarrytown and is a parvo survivor. She's pretty big in comparison, but Claudelie couldn't care less. She immediately started following Cookie around and mimicking what she does. She's gentle with our cats. When they hiss at her, she moves away. It's been about four days and they're used to her, which is a really quick transition. She's smart, but not yet house-trained. We've been working on it. She's good about going in her crate and does not whine when we put her in it for the night. I think she will have some separation anxiety and might resource guard. I think the resource guarding is something she can get over. She's just not used to having anything.

Model alert! Ozzie is a gorgeous and fluffy chocolate brown splendor with stunning amber eyes and a loving heart. memos.Disclaimer:
The dog you are adopting or fostering has been rescued from one of our more under-resourced partner shelters and unfortunately has come to us with ticks on them. Rest assured that upon their arrival they were treated with Nexgard which will kill fleas within hours and the ticks within 24-48 hours. Often the dead tick will detach on its own, but not always and might require removal.

We understand that this can be concerning to bring into your home, but we have some ideas that have worked for other fosters and adopters previously. In order to limit the spreading of the ticks while they are dying we recommend keeping the dog in a spare bathroom, bedroom or a x-pen area for this initial period. This will help with clean-up if they are in a smaller space where it is easier to clean up afterwards. Additionally, baths can help with removing the ticks! Just be aware that after the first bath you’ll want to use water only so you aren’t stripping your dog’s coat of their naturally occurring oils which could make them itchy.

If you have any concerns about your resident dog getting ticks from your foster or adopted dog, please let us know and we can provide a single dose of tick meds for them as well while your new APA! dog is getting rid of their ticks.

memos.Behavior Team FFU:
[return request] Fosters said our previous advice had helped, but GC was still too much for them. Asked info gathering questions.

8/9 from the foster (dog has since been adopted!): How does Good Charlotte do meeting new people in your home? In public?: She is friendly and seems to love people. The only thing we have to warn people about is her tendency to jump up.
Has she been around kids and if so how does she do? What about dogs? Cats?: We don't have kids, and I don't think she'll be aggressive, but I would avoid a house with kids (or at least young kids) just because of the jumping up and sometimes mouthing when she gets excited. She's done this a lot less since the first day we got her, but given her size and strength, this might be difficult to manage with little ones. Dogs it's hard to say for sure because we haven't really introduced her to other dogs besides our resident dog. She plays rough and doesn't know when to stop playing, so I think a house with dogs isn't a deal breaker, but it should be either a calm dog that won't hype her up or an equally active dog who can keep up with her. Our dog is usually chill alone, but will also want to play constantly if she's around and they're a bit different in size and age, so we feel a need to constantly monitor them when they're together -- this is one of the major factors that made us decide to seek a foster take-over. And cats, only ones that are used to an energetic dog. She was very curious about a stray cat in our neighborhood and it jumped up at her, so that also might've made her nervous around cats now.
How does she do when left home alone?: We keep her in a room with an open crate, and she is mostly fine but will whine and paw at the door initially, so this could be problematic for someone living in an apartment. We have her on a pretty strict schedule to get her more used to being alone (in her room from 9-12, 1-5, and bed at 8:30). She sleeps through most of her alone time, but does have periods of boredom in that 1-5pm stretch where she will whine, although she is mostly good at not reverting to destruction. She is a strong chewer, but only chewed through her toys, leash, and her bed (now we only leave a blanket in her crate along with toys that won't easily be chewed through), so while I wouldn't feel comfortable letting her have free range of a house alone yet, she at least hasn't reverted to chewing things like the walls or furniture.
Are there any specific behavioral issues you have experienced that would be important for future adopters to know? If so, can you describe those please?: I think the main thing is her energy and tendency to jump and mouth especially when she is either over excited or tired and trying to fight it. An adopter with an active lifestyle and a home with a backyard would probably be best as it helps get some of her energy out. Outside of that, it's just that she is and still behaves like a puppy, so going in with that expectation will help. She was listed as 3 years old when we picked her up, so I don't think we were mentally prepared for this. She has improved though, she just needs someone who is either more experienced at training a puppy than we are or someone who is looking to dedicate time to learn and grow with her.

animals.name: Tony the Tiger
animals.kennelCardMemo:
Tony the Tiger: A Brave Little Companion Ready for His Stripes

True to his name, Tony the Tiger has shown the resilience of a survivor. He is currently recovering from an old, severe head injury that likely resulted from a dog bite before he came into shelter care. Because the injury went untreated for some time, his damaged left eye could not be saved, and the area was surgically closed to allow him to fully heal. Despite this physical change, Tony is adjusting well and is looking for a patient foster family to support him through his final stages of recovery.

This young pup is naturally cheerful and possesses a playful, puppy-like energy. He is active and fun-loving, proving daily that his interest in the world around him is intact. Tony is also affectionate with his human caretakers and will reliably snooze in his crate when it is time to rest after spending time together.

Tony has already spent time in a foster home where he coexisted comfortably with other dogs, making him a suitable match for a household with existing social pets. He is neutered and at a young, manageable age where he can keep up on daily walks while remaining easy to handle. Welcoming Tony into your home provides this resilient pup with the quiet, safe space he needs to complete his healing journey.

Tony the Tiger suffered a severe bite injury to his head that caused suspected skull fractures, infected wounds/abscesses, and loss of his left eye. Despite these serious injuries, he was alert, walking normally, and otherwise stable at his exam; he will remain permanently blind on the left side, and his longer-term prognosis depends on how well the infection and skull injuries heal. Tony is receiving doxycycline for infection, carprofen for pain and inflammation, and gabapentin for pain; medications are currently prescribed through July 31, 2026, and no refills are documented, so they should be given exactly as labeled. He is scheduled for a sedated clinic appointment on July 22, 2026, to thoroughly clean the wounds and possibly surgically close the empty left eye socket, with additional follow-up based on those findings.

memos.Medical Consult:
Tony the Tiger is a sweet young dog who is recovering from surgery after an old, severe head injury that likely resulted from a dog bite. His damaged left eye could not be saved, so the area was surgically closed, and he was also neutered. After surgery, he had several episodes of bleeding from his neuter incision and was found to have a low platelet count, so he is being treated with prednisone (through 8/14/2026) along with omeprazole (through 8/11/2026) to help protect his stomach while on steroids. He should have an in-person recheck around 8/8/2026 to assess whether the bleeding has resolved and determine if his prednisone can be safely tapered; seek veterinary care sooner if he develops new bleeding, pale gums, severe lethargy, or other concerning signs. His prognosis is fair to good if the bleeding and platelet issue resolve as expected, and he has otherwise been bright, eating well, and recovering nicely.

Please see the medical record for the complete medical history. This is only a synopsis of the most important information. 8/2/26 TH

animals.name: Milli Vanilli
animals.kennelCardMemo:
Gentle, Chill, Happy

Meet Milli Vanilli! Unlike his namesake, you can be assured there is no lip-synching. When he sings the song of his people, those vocals belong to him!

Milli is a sweet, calm kitty who was recently rescued from the July floods. He is still getting comfortable in his foster home, but has already shown himself to be a kind and loving kitty. We think he is working his way up to cuddles by the way he enjoys getting pets, especially around his ears, and likes to walk near your legs and feet.

Milli is currently being kept in the bathroom of his foster home to give him time to adjust to his new environment one room at a time. This sweet boy cries at night unless a light is kept on in his room. It must be scary being alone in the dark after all he has been through. He is so tidy around the litterbox that he will sweep the floor with his paws to clean up any kitty litter - such a polite gentleman!

Milli’s orange tabby coat has lovely stripes in front and on the top of his head and amazing swirls of cream and orange on his side and back. He is stunning and such a pleasure to pet. The sweetest creamsicle kitty you’ll find!

Milli was initially frightened by the 4-year-old in his foster home. She’s a fast mover, which is a bit much after the upheaval he’s been through. But, he is getting more comfortable around this energetic little human every day.

Milli is a gentle, lovely cat who would be a wonderful addition to a family or person who would enjoy the company of a mellow kitty and who will give him the chance to get comfortable at his own speed. He has a social, easygoing nature which is sure to blossom magnificently with patience, nurturing and time.

If you would like to welcome Milli to your home and give him the love he so richly deserves, contact us for an introduction!

All APA! cats are fully vetted, spayed or neutered, and have updated vaccines and a microchip. Lifetime support is offered by our Cat Behavior Team.

For further information or to meet Milli Vanilli, please email adopt@austinpetsalive.org

Snuggly, Courageous, Loving

Sandy aka Cosmic Cocoa is a total cuddle bug who just wants to be wherever her people are. She settled into her foster home almost immediately and was quick to start purring and soaking up all the pets. She especially loves cheek scratches, and if you stop petting her too soon, she'll gently rub against you to ask for more

With a low-key energy level, Sandy would much rather spend her day snuggled up beside you than chasing toys. She gets along well with other cats but would prefer a home without dogs, as they make her nervous. While she hasn't been around children in foster care, her gentle personality suggests she'd likely do well with respectful kids. Sandy came to APA! after the Uvalde floods and has proven to be incredibly resilient, sweet, and trusting. If you're looking for a loving companion who never gets tired of cuddles, Sandy is your girl.

All APA! cats are fully vetted, spayed or neutered, and have updated vaccines and a microchip. Lifetime support is offered by our Cat Behavior Team.

animals.name: Cool Cube
animals.kennelCardMemo:
Seeing a transformation happen right before your eyes is a truly beautiful thing, and this sweet girl is a shining example of a fresh start. When Cool Cube first arrived, she was quite thin and her coat was looking a bit fair and worn. With some steady care, good nutrition, and time to decompress in her foster home, she has blossomed wonderfully. Today, she boasts a healthy, good coat that shows off her rich brindle patterns, and her bright, happy posture says it all. She is a silly, goofy girl who absolutely loves to play, welcoming visitors with an approachable, companionable attitude.

This athletic young dog is highly treat-motivated, making her a star student during training sessions. She already works well with a clicker and food rewards, successfully practicing basic commands. She is already both house trained and crate trained, making her transition into a household routine much smoother. She maintains a moderate energy level and travels with a loose leash on walks. When it is time to wind down or when she is left alone, she settles nicely, sleeps comfortably in her crate at night, and rests quietly there during the day.

Because she prefers to have her own dedicated space, she does best keeping her toys and bones to herself, and she likes to have her kennel area respected by other pets. Her previous caretakers note that she could potentially live with another household dog if given a very patient, gradual introduction. With her health on a great track, her striking coat looking better than ever, and a heart full of goofy fun, she is completely ready to transition into a permanent routine.

Cool Cube is ready to bring her healthy new look and playful spirit straight to your home! Meet this wonderful girl today and see if she is the perfect match for you.

She is also a step ahead on the homefront, already bringing the excellent foundation of being house-trained and crate-trained to the table. If you are ready to hit the jackpot of companionship and add a resilient, fun-loving friend to your daily routine, she is ready to bring the luck. Meet Clover and bring her home today.

memos.Disclaimer:
The dog you are adopting or fostering has been rescued from one of our more under-resourced partner shelters and unfortunately has come to us with ticks on them. Rest assured that upon their arrival they were treated with Nexgard which will kill fleas within hours and the ticks within 24-48 hours. Often the dead tick will detach on its own, but not always and might require removal.

We understand that this can be concerning to bring into your home, but we have some ideas that have worked for other fosters and adopters previously. In order to limit the spreading of the ticks while they are dying we recommend keeping the dog in a spare bathroom, bedroom or a x-pen area for this initial period. This will help with clean-up if they are in a smaller space where it is easier to clean up afterwards. Additionally, baths can help with removing the ticks! Just be aware that after the first bath you’ll want to use water only so you aren’t stripping your dog’s coat of their naturally occurring oils which could make them itchy.

If you have any concerns about your resident dog getting ticks from your foster or adopted dog, please let us know and we can provide a single dose of tick meds for them as well while your new APA! dog is getting rid of their ticks.

animals.name: Rhonda
animals.kennelCardMemo:
With a joyful smile and a heart full of love, Rhonda is ready to sing her way right into your life. She is a true people-oriented companion who thrives on human connection, warmth, and quality time together. Whether you are relaxing after a long day or simply hanging out around the house, this sweet girl is always eager to be right by your side, offering steady companionship and a wagging tail. She has a natural charm that makes everyone she meets feel special, and her affectionate nature makes her an excellent partner for anyone looking for a loyal, devoted friend.

When it comes to downtime, Rhonda is an absolute expert at cuddling. She loves nothing more than curling up close, leaning in for pets, and soaking up all the affection you are willing to give. While she is a wonderfully affectionate couch sidekick, she also possesses an impressive, athletic curiosity and a clever mind. Because she is smart and determined enough to scale a standard fence when left to her own devices, she will do best with supervised outdoor time or on-leash adventures where you can explore the world together safely. She is a well-rounded companion who balances her adventurous, bright spirit with a deeply loving soul.

"Help me, Rhonda, help me get out of the shelter and into your heart!" If you are ready to add a splash of harmony and a whole lot of love to your home, come say hello and bring this wonderful girl home today.

memos.Foster Notes:
"How long was your Sleepover
5 days so far but ongoing

Select at least three traits that best describe this dog:
Athletic
Calm
Affectionate
Chill

What made you smile or laugh about them?
Kamaya is constantly entertaining with her curiosity and enthusiasm for learning about the wide world. She examines a new thing very daintily with her nose, tongue, and teeth. This includes treats. No wolfing down for this gal. Her elegant demeanor is broken at times by zoomies and exuberance. It’s hard not to be amused by her athletic antics, leaping from one piece of furniture to another like a mountain goat, but she is learning what is acceptable and what is a bit too much.

Is there anything a future adopter should know to set them up for success?
She should not, at least now when she’s so young, be around little kids. But she has never resource guarded here, and lets us take away food or something she’s not supposed to be chewing without objection. She needs a lot of mental stimulation and action to wear her out. She is definitely not “on” all the time and can chill at your feet quite readily while you work from home. The one area where she is timid is around cars and the street. And we’re working on that, going out on leash to just hang out near the house. At first she would shy away from any car going by and struggle to escape her collar with the old trick of letting the choke collar go slack, then twisting out of it. Now she stands, trembling but not struggling and allows herself to be petted and loved on. I feel certain she will soon figure out how interesting and fun it is to go for walkies. And then, for someone other than me, to start her training to be a running companion.

Where did the dog sleep
Other

How was the dog in the car?
Some whining or pacing, but settled

How was the dog when left alone?
Not left alone

What is their housetraining status?
Fully housetrained - Consistently holds it when left alone, and gives clear signals when they need to go outside. May have had accidents in the first couple days, but leveled out completely once the dog learned the routines.

How did the dog do in the bath?
Did not attempt to give the dog a bath

How did they do with other adults in the home or visitors? Did they meet visitors, or only hang with you?
Loved everyone

How did they do with cats or small animals (if present)?
Not applicable

How did they do with children (if present)?
No children present

How did they do with other dogs (if present)?
Loved them

How would you describe their energy level?
High

How were they on leash?
Pulled sometimes

Would you adopt this dog if you could? Why or why not?
The only reason I’m not keeping her is I’m so devoted to heelers, I’m waiting for one to show up. Kamaya is so smart and so athletic and so absolutely beautiful she would be a real catch for someone who wants a dog to turn heads on the trail and who will be good with other dogs and people. She is small (for a husky), very soft fur, very affectionate. She would be a love bug companion for an outdoorsy, athletic woman."
memos.Behavior Consult: Touched base with adopter who is also s/o host.  She was given BC at the time of placement and has not seen any concerning behaviors so far.  She did note that Kamaya is energetic and mouthy so wondering if that might have played into the incident with the younger child, but is comfortable with the information.  Let her know that she had BT support if she did start seeing behaviors and wanted support in the future.-MC
memos.Behavior Team FFU:
[Bite Incident] [RETURN] FTA emailed last night reporting "I am reaching out regarding an incident that happened this evening with Kamaya. My 18 month old son was trying to play with her toy and she gave several warning barks/snips but when he walked past her later, she bit him on the face. Then he was quite a while away walking and she lunged at him again. I’m unsure where to call or what to do but I’m nervous a more serious incident may occur as she gets more comfortable. She’s fine with my 3 year old but suddenly got defensive and aggressive with my 18 month old. Were surprised since she’s been beyond playful and calm since we met her. Please let me know what to do next."

Dog Support team replied initially advising that they keep Kamaya separated from the kids. I followed up this morning reiterating that they keep Kamaya and both kids separated until we know more. I sent bite questions and additional questions about the incident. Offered a phone call if that is easier. AKC

*UPDATE: Sleepover host replied providing more details about the bite incident to her 18 month old son. The bite did not break the skin, it left a small red mark that faded away completely with a little time. The female sleepover host was sitting on the couch and Kamaya was on the couch next to her with a toy. Their 18 month old son was standing on the ground with his hands on the couch. He was initially reaching towards the toy that Kamaya had and she first quickly covered the toy with her front paws and then gave a quick growl and air snap in his direction. The boy started to turn towards his mom and move towards her when Kamaya quickly lunged forward biting him on the cheek. It was a very fast nip and she just laid there afterwards. The mom picked up her son and was checking him. A minute later the boy was set back on the ground and tried to walk past Kamaya who was still on the couch but was no longer actively playing with the toy. As the boy passed she again tried to lunge towards him but no contact was made. The male sleepover host came over and put Kamaya in the crate and they kept her separated from the kids after that. The female sleepover host said that the next day while Kamaya was crate the boys (18 month old and 3 yr old) were walking near the crate and Kamaya low growled briefly. Prior to that she had no negative reactions around the 3 yr old.

I spoke in person with the male sleepover host when he physically returned Kamaya. He had been sitting at the dining table facing the living room when the incident happened. He said that he didn't feel uncomfortable with Kamaya's behavior leading up to the bite and that he was willing to keep working with her but his wife was too nervous and not comfortable trying to make it work. I'm choosing not to add a resource guarding (RG) attribute at this time because there is not enough evidence to support that RG was the reason for Kamaya's reaction. It is possible she was not as comfortable with the youngest child. Adding a BC and child score 3 to indicate that slightly older kids might be better. AKC

animals.kennelCardMemo:
Meet a handsome 3-year-old German Shepherd who brings together everything people love about the breed: intelligence, loyalty, playful energy, and a huge heart. He enjoys meeting new people and is always ready to make a new friend, especially when cuddles might be involved.

In his foster home, he has been fully house trained and gets along well with other dogs. He is also remarkably quiet—his foster has yet to hear him bark! He settles nicely into a home routine and has shown that he can be an easy, enjoyable companion.

This playful guy loves long walks and would be thrilled to join someone who enjoys exploring the neighborhood or heading out on daily adventures. Exercise helps him burn off his youthful energy, and once he has had a good walk, he is perfectly content to relax and recharge.

One of his favorite pastimes is lounging by a window and watching the world go by. Whether he is observing people, cars, or neighborhood activity, he is happy to take it all in from his favorite viewing spot before settling in for a nap.

Most of all, he is a complete cuddle fanatic. He does not simply sit beside you—he leans his whole body in, wraps his paws around you like a hug, and gazes up with the sweetest, most loving expression. His goofy, enthusiastic way of showing affection is impossible to resist, and he is ready to give one lucky family all the hugs they can handle.

Sleepover hosts describe Wheat Thin as a sweet and affectionate companion who loves being near his people and leaning in close for quiet company. Wheat Thin has shown that he LOVES people. LOVES. THEM. He's such a people pleaser and wants to show every person he's met how good he can be. Coming from a rural shelter, Wheat Thin is still learning what it means to be in a home, so he's a little anxious to be on his own. "Flight Risk" is a term used to describe when dogs who may have a strong tendency to escape or run away when they feel scared, anxious, bored, or overstimulated. This behavior can be triggered by loud noises, unfamiliar environments, lack of engagement, something desirable, or even a sudden movement. While dogs are transitioning into a new environment or home, there is a higher likelihood to see escape attempts.

Specific Behavior: Sleepover host noted that he pulled hard on leash in reaction to loud noises. Additionally the host noted that escaped a wire crate.

Strategies for Managing and Supporting Dogs who Present a Flight Risk
- Secure Environment: Ensure that your home and yard are escape-proof. This means checking fences for any gaps or weaknesses, making sure gates latch securely, and being mindful of any potential escape routes. Consider adding additional barriers, like baby gates or temporary fencing, to further secure the area.
- Leash and Tethering: Keep a drag leash clipped to your dog’s collar for at least the first month while your dog is acclimating to their new home. When outside, always keep your dog on a leash, even in a fenced yard, until you are confident in their ability to stay within the boundaries. Do not leave them unattended when outside. A double-leash system (using both a harness and a collar) can provide extra security during walks, and a martingale collar will prevent him from being able to slip out and away. Avoid using a retractable leash, as they can easily break.
- Safe Entry and Exit: Be cautious when opening doors, as many flight-risk dogs may seize any opportunity to dart outside. Teach your dog to wait calmly before doors are opened, and set up gates or other air lock systems around exterior doors and gates to prevent door darting. When going on car rides, tether his leash outside of the door to ensure you can get a firm hold on it before opening the door. Do not leave windows open in the car during car rides, and never allow him to be off-leash in public.
- Identification & Tracking: Ensure your dog is always wearing a collar with up-to-date identification tags. Microchipping is also highly recommended as an additional layer of security, as well as attaching an Apple Airtag to their collar.
- Training and Positive Reinforcement: Work on building a strong recall response within him where he will reliably return to you when prompted.

memos.Disclaimer:
"On-leash reactivity"(OLR) is a term used to describe when a dog has a heightened reaction to things they encounter when on-leash, typically when they see another animal, person, or moving object. There are several reasons dogs can develop leash reactivity:
- Excitement or Frustration: Some dogs become frustrated because the leash prevents them from reaching another dog or person they want to interact with, and prevents them from using their natural social cues, like retreating or approaching in a controlled manner.
- Fear or Anxiety: Others may be fearful or anxious and feel the need to defend themselves because the leash makes them feel trapped.
- Overstimulation: For some dogs, too much stimulation - whether it’s from people, other dogs, or environmental factors - can overwhelm them, causing them to react.

The behavior may look different from dog to dog, and can range from barking and lunging to growling or pulling toward the object of their focus. It doesn’t mean the dog is aggressive, but rather that they are reacting in a heightened way due to the feelings they have developed around constraints of the leash.

Specific Behavior: Will sometimes pull, bark and lunge towards other dogs while out on walks. Has done well with training and is improving with this

Strategies for Managing and Supporting Dogs with OLR
- Desensitization and Counter-Conditioning: Gradually expose your dog to their triggers in a controlled and positive manner. Start at a distance where your dog doesn’t feel the need to react and slowly decrease the distance over time, rewarding them for remaining calm. If you notice a trigger approaching, calmly cross the street, make a turn, or increase the distance to help your dog stay under threshold (the point at which they begin to react).
- Proper Walking Equipment: Tools like front-clip harnesses or head halters can give you more control over your dog while minimizing pulling and lunging.
- Controlled Walks: When walking your dog, choose quiet, low-traffic routes where you’re less likely to encounter the triggers that might cause reactivity, so your dog can have positive, calm experiences on the leash without becoming overwhelmed. 
- Avoid Punishment: Never punish a dog for leash reactivity. Punishment can increase their anxiety or frustration and worsen the behavior. Instead, focus on teaching them what TO do (remain calm, focus on you) rather than what NOT to do.
